newsitem.title: PERU: Peru constitutional court head quits in protest.
newsitem.headline: Peru constitutional court head quits in protest.

text.p: The head of Peru's highest constitutional court resigned on Friday to protest against Congress' dismissal of three court members who were blocking a possible third election bid by President Alberto Fujimori.
"This court was the last hope and bastion of legality and respect for the constitutional law," judge Ricardo Nugent said at a news conference called to announce his departure.

His resignation, though widely expected, brought to a head a long-running confrontation between Fujimori's government and the Constitutional Tribunal, which has theoretical autonomy over all constitutional matters in Peru.
It also left the seven-member court with only three sitting judges when four are needed for a quorum.
"Congress did not take a legal decision but a political one," Nugent told the news conference. "I am convinced there is more behind this."
The government-controlled Congress dismissed on Thursday three of the judges who had cast doubt on a new law clearing the way for Fujimori to run again for president in 2000.

The legislature's decision unleashed a wave of protest from opposition parties, local media and the Peruvian public. It was widely perceived as an abuse of power by the government and an act of vengeance against the court.

Fujimori has not commented on the issue, but his economy minister, Jorge Camet, said on Friday Congress had acted within its rights and would seek to replace the dismissed judges. "Isn't that democracy?" he asked on local radio.
Fujimori won a surprise election victory in 1990 and re-election by a landslide in 1995. But Peruvian law is ambiguous on whether he is eligible for a third term.

The three dismissed judges and Nugent had issued two separate rulings on a government-sponsored law designed to permit Fujimori's candidacy. Their interpretations left the president with an insecure legal platform from which to launch his campaign.

The Constitutional Tribunal has existed for less than a year. Its predecessor, the Constitutional Guarantees Tribunal, was abolished when Fujimori seized extraordinary powers in 1992 in a so-called self-coup.

The re-election dispute has quickly soured the political atmosphere in Peru after a brief period of euphoria caused by the end of a four-month hostage crisis provoked by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).

Critics say that in moving against the court, Fujimori took advantage of the boost given his popularity by the military assault that killed all the MRTA hostage-takers and freed almost all their captives. One of the 72 hostages and two soldiers were killed in the assault.
